title: Water, Life, Heat, Writing
objectives: I can break a word into its roots and use them to predict its meaning.
I can explain what aqua, bio, therm, and graph mean and name words that use each one.
I can use a root I know to work out a new science word.
I can write about a science trip using ten words built from Greek and Latin roots.
rationale: Aqua, bio, therm, and graph each appear in dozens of science and social studies words, and each is stable and easy to see in the spelling. The unit teaches the four roots through ten words that students will meet in science class, so a student who learns aqua, therm, or graph can unlock words never taught directly. It builds on tele-, micro-, and scope from unit 3 (graph returns from telegraph) and uses the science vocabulary of predator and prey as a base for biology. The method is the point: find the root, say what it means, predict the word, then check the prediction in context. The passage follows a class hunting for roots at a science museum so students see each root in a real setting.

passage.title: Four Roots at the Science Museum
paras: Ms. Park's class visited the science museum, and she handed each student a card listing four roots: aqua for water, bio for life, therm for heat, and graph for write or draw. "Hunt for words that use them," she said. In the first hall, Leo pressed his nose to the glass of a giant aquarium. "These aquatic animals spend their whole lives in water," he read from the sign.

Upstairs, a model of a Roman aqueduct curved across a table. A guide explained that Roman builders used these bridge-like channels to carry fresh water into their cities. "Aqua for water, duct for a channel," Leo whispered, and he checked it off his card.

In the biology lab, a scientist showed how living things are studied. On her shelf sat a biography of an explorer who mapped rivers. A thermometer on the wall read seventy degrees, and she pointed to a thermostat that kept the room from getting too hot or too cold. "Heat words are everywhere," she said, "even on the thermal mug I use to keep my tea warm."

Before the class left, the scientist signed Leo's card with her autograph. Next to it, Leo sketched a graphic of the whole trip, with a fish, an arch, and a thermometer, each labeled with its root. "You are reading words like a scientist," Ms. Park said.

teacher.overview: Students learn four roots through ten science words: aqua (water), bio (life), therm (heat), and graph (write, draw). The passage is a museum trip where a class hunts for roots, which models the method students will use: spot the root, say its meaning, predict the word, and check in context. Writing asks students to apply the roots to a place they could visit.

notes.va.aquatic.adj: Aquatic is an adjective for things in or on water. Contrast with marine (ocean) so students see that lakes and rivers are aquatic too. Have students predict aquatic from aqua before showing the definition.
notes.va.aquarium.n: An aquarium is both a tank and a building. Both senses are fine here. Note that the ending -arium means a place for something, so students can predict other places with that ending.
notes.va.aqueduct.n: An aqueduct carries water, often across a gap. Students may associate Roman aqueducts with arches only. Ask what the word would mean without the arches, and have them guess aqua plus duct before looking up the word.
notes.va.biography.n: A biography is the story of a real person's life told by someone else. Contrast with autobiography, a life story written by the person. Ask students to explain why bio plus graph builds the meaning.
notes.va.biology.n: Biology is the study of living things, and the ending -logy means study of. Link to predator and prey from unit 5 as part of biology. Students can list other -logy words, such as zoology.
notes.va.thermometer.n: Thermometer joins therm (heat) and meter (measure). Compare with other measuring words such as barometer. Ask students to read a real thermometer in class and say the temperature in a full sentence.
notes.va.thermal.adj: Thermal is an adjective meaning of heat or holding heat. Students may know thermal underwear or a thermal mug. Remind them that thermal is not about cold; it is about heat and how it moves or stays.
notes.va.thermostat.n: A thermostat keeps temperature steady by turning heat on and off. Contrast with a thermometer: one measures, one controls. A diagram with two boxes, measure and control, helps students sort.
notes.va.autograph.n: An autograph is a person's own signature, and auto- means self. Students sometimes mix it with a printed name. Emphasize written in the person's own hand. Link to graph (write) and telegraph from unit 3.
notes.va.graphic.adj: Graphic here means shown in drawings, charts, or pictures, as in a graphic organizer. Some students know another sense, vivid and shocking, as in a graphic description. Teach the picture sense and mention that graphic can also describe very detailed or upsetting descriptions.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see the word thermostat. I know therm means heat from thermometer. I do not know stat, but the scientist says it kept the room from getting too hot or too cold. So a thermostat must control heat. I can check by asking what stat adds: staying steady. Therm plus stat makes a heat-steadier.'

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit telescope, microscope, predator, and prey by sorting them with the new words into two groups: tools that help us see or measure, and words about living things. Return to the four roots after two days, again at one week, with a root hunt in textbooks.

frames: I read a biography about ___ because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A gives a root (aqua, bio, therm, or graph). Partner B names a word with that root and says what the word means in a sentence.

needsReview: Root meanings (aqua = water, bio = life, therm = heat, graph = write or draw, meter = measure, duct = channel or carry, stat = staying) are standard Greek and Latin roots but the word-family claims and spelling changes (aqua -> aque, aqua -> aqu, ic -> tic) have not been checked against an etymological dictionary.
Spanish glosses (acuático, acuario, acueducto, biografía, biología, termómetro, térmico, termostato, autógrafo, gráfico) are standard cognates but have not been reviewed by a native speaker.

Passage facts: Roman builders used aqueducts to carry water into cities; a thermostat keeps room temperature steady; both are standard but not checked against a cited source. The explorer's biography and the science museum scene are invented.
